title: Northern Yuan
capsule: The Northern Yuan (Mongolian: ᠬᠣᠶᠢᠲᠤ ᠶᠤᠸᠠᠨ ᠤᠯᠤᠰ / Khoit Yuan) was the rump Mongol regime that carried the Borjigin imperial court onto the steppe after the Ming drove the Yuan from China proper in 1368. In this period its Chinggisid khans—Biligtü, Uskhal Tögüs Temür, then a rapid succession from Yesüder through Adai Khan (d. 1438)—nominally claimed the Yuan mandate, but after Tögüs Temür's death in 1388 the Han-style "Great Yuan" title was abandoned and real power passed to tribal kingmakers. The Ming launched repeated northern campaigns, including the Yongle Emperor's personal expeditions and the fighting around the Kherlen River in 1409, while the western Oirats rose to dominance: Mahmud and then Toghan installed and deposed khans, crushed their eastern rival Arughtai by 1434, and by the late 1430s set the stage for Toghan's son Esen Taishi to eclipse Chinggisid authority entirely.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Territorial extent is highly uncertain; the Northern Yuan controlled the Mongolian steppe but exact range expanded and contracted with Oirat versus Chinggisid power. Boundaries are reconstructed from Chinese frontier records and secondary literature on Inner Asian history, with low precision.
